1.c4 g6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight towards d5 and e4 and keeps every plan open: a broad centre with e4 and d4, a fianchetto with g3, or d4 alone against Black's set-up. The knight stands on the long diagonal of Black's coming bishop, so White must reckon with ...Bxc3 and doubled c-pawns.

1.c4 g6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn at once and steers the game towards 1.d4 structures with c4 as extra space. The cost is a target: Black's fianchettoed bishop bears down on d4, so the pawn needs support, and Black can strike at the centre later with a pawn break.

1.c4 g6 2.e4.strategy: Builds the classical pawn centre: the pawns on c4 and e4 clamp d5 and give White the space. White needs d4 and a knight to turn it into an advantage, while Black's counterplay aims at d4 and the dark squares with the fianchettoed bishop.

1.c4 g6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, whose diagonal supports e4 and presses on the queenside, while the centre pawns stay undecided. Solid and flexible, but it concedes central space: Black can mirror the set-up or claim the middle first.

1.c4 g6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight and covers d4 and e5 without committing a pawn, so White keeps the choice between a fianchetto set-up and a central build-up. The cost is that White has no central pawn yet, so Black may choose the structure.

1.c4 g6 2.d3.strategy: Prepares e4 and opens the c1-bishop, keeping a flexible set-up. It leaves d4 unclaimed, so Black can build a pawn centre of their own. Sound, but slower than the principled developing moves.

1.c4 g6 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and prepares d4, but the c1-bishop stays shut in by the d2-pawn and no pawn takes the centre. Sound but passive: Black can take central space and choose the structure.

1.c4 g6 2.a3.strategy: Prepares b4 for queenside space, but leaves the centre and development untouched, so Black simply claims the central squares.

1.c4 g6 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space but does nothing for the centre or development, and it leaves b4 weak. Black develops undisturbed.

1.c4 g6 2.b3.strategy: Opens the long diagonal for Black: after 2...Bg7 the bishop eyes the rook on a1, and the natural 3.Bb2 loses a piece to 3...Bxb2 because nothing recaptures, so White must first block the diagonal and the fianchetto plan is delayed.

1.c4 g6 2.b4.strategy: Overextends the queenside: after 2...Bg7 the rook on a1 is attacked and 3.Bb2 loses a piece to 3...Bxb2, while the b4-pawn becomes a target for ...a5. The advance does nothing for the centre or development.

1.c4 g6 2.f3.strategy: Takes f3 from the king's knight and weakens the e1-h4 diagonal. It only makes sense with a pawn centre to follow; meanwhile Black develops and challenges the centre at once.

1.c4 g6 2.f4.strategy: Grabs kingside space and controls e5, but opens the e1-h4 diagonal to the king before White has a pawn in the centre. Black develops freely and hits the centre at leisure.

1.c4 g6 2.g4.strategy: Advances the g-pawn without support: ...d6 threatens ...Bxg4 because the queen cannot recapture through e2, and ...h5 undermines it at once. It also loosens f4, h4 and the long diagonal with the king still in the centre.

1.c4 g6 2.h3.strategy: A slow prophylactic move against a later ...Bg4 that does nothing for the centre or development; Black develops and takes the initiative.

1.c4 g6 2.h4.strategy: Aims for h5 to open the h-file against Black's fianchetto, but Black can cover h5 or take the square first, and the advance does nothing for the centre. The h-pawn can never again guard g3 or g4.

1.c4 g6 2.Na3.strategy: A rim knight that eyes c2 and b5 but is far from the centre and hampers the a-pawn; Black takes central space unhindered.

1.c4 g6 2.Qc2.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece has moved, guarding c4 and eyeing e4, but it has no target. Black develops while White's minor pieces are still at home.

1.c4 g6 2.Qb3.strategy: Presses on b7, a pawn the c8-bishop guards, so there is no threat, and the diagonal to f7 is blocked by White's own c4-pawn. Black develops freely while the queen has no target.

1.c4 g6 2.Qa4.strategy: Pins the d7-pawn against the king until Black blocks with ...c6 or ...Nc6, but has no real target, since d7 and a7 are well guarded. Black develops while the queen does nothing for White's pieces still at home.

1.c4 g6 2.Nh3.strategy: Puts a knight on the rim aiming at f4 and g5, but after ...d6 the c8-bishop threatens ...Bxh3, which would leave White with doubled h-pawns after gxh3 and a weakened kingside.

1.c4 g6 2.c5.strategy: Gains space but pushes the c-pawn a second time and gives up control of d5. ...d6 challenges it at once, and after cxd6 Black recaptures and has an open centre and easy development.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 Bg7.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal against d4 and b2 and prepares to castle, while keeping every set-up open. The price is that White holds the bigger centre first, and Black must undermine it later.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and controls e4 and d5. Together with ...g6 it reaches the set-ups of the King's Indian and the Grünfeld, sharp and rich in theory. White gets the big centre first, and Black's counterplay depends on striking at it in time.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 d6.strategy: Controls e5, frees the c8-bishop and keeps the knight's development flexible, so Black can still choose between a set-up with ...Nf6 and one that holds the knight back. The d-pawn is committed early, which rules out striking at the centre with ...d5, and White decides how much space to take.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 f5.strategy: Takes e4 and aims for a Dutch-style set-up with the bishop on g7 and quick castling. But the pawn loosens the kingside and leaves e6 unguarded, and White can press at once with a flank push such as 3.h4. Playable, not a move to learn.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 Na6.strategy: Guards c5 and b4 and keeps Black's usual plans available, but the knight on the rim does nothing about d4 and c4 and blocks the a-pawn. White takes more space, and Black must still find a way to undermine the centre. Sound enough, but White gets a free hand.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5, but 3.e4 takes that square away, since the pawn would capture the knight there, and leaves the knight on the rim without a job. White gets a broad centre with tempo, and the knight belongs on f6.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to go with ...Bg7, a double-fianchetto set-up that aims at d4 and e4 from the wings. White simply takes the centre, and Black must then undermine it. Sound, but it gives White time to build.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn chain while the kingside pieces are still to come. It commits the c-pawn early and takes c6 from the b8-knight, so Black's play is sound but passive against White's broad centre.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once for a Benoni- or Sicilian-type game with ...Bg7 to come. If White takes on c5, Black regains the pawn but loses time with the queen; if White pushes d5, White gets space in a Benoni-type structure. Playable, but White chooses the structure.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 and a flexible set-up, but the e6-pawn shuts in the c8-bishop. White can play 3.e4 at once, and ...Nf6 is then met by e5, so Black must strike at the centre quickly. Sound but slow.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight, but 3.d5 attacks it at once and leaves it no good square: on e5 it is soon driven off by pawns, on b4 by a3. White gains space and tempi while the f8-bishop is still at home.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 Bh6.strategy: Attacks the c1-bishop, but 3.Bxh6 Nxh6 trades off the fianchetto bishop that ...g6 was played for. Black is left with weak dark squares and a loose knight on h6, which 4.Qd2 attacks at once.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5, but a flank pawn move develops nothing and leaves the centre to White. Black's pieces are still at home, while White builds a full centre at leisure.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 a5.strategy: Takes b4 and gains space on the queenside, but it ignores the centre and weakens b5. White builds freely while Black's pieces are still at home.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Strikes at c4 at once. After 3.cxd5 only ...Nf6 holds, and then Black regains the pawn with a fair game; ...Qxd5 loses a tempo to Nc3. Sound, but it asks Black to know the follow-up, and White chooses the structure.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 f6.strategy: Takes e5 from White's pieces and prepares ...e5, but it blocks the long diagonal of the future g7-bishop and the f6 square for the knight. White builds the centre and holds more space.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 h6.strategy: Wastes a tempo on a rim pawn that contests neither c4 nor d4. The pawn is safe, since 3.Bxh6 Bxh6 loses the bishop for it, but White builds the centre while Black's pieces stay at home.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 h5.strategy: Weakens g5 for good and develops nothing: a bishop on g5 can no longer be challenged by ...h6. White uses the tempo to build the centre, and the h-pawn does no work on the kingside.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 b5.strategy: Hangs a pawn: 3.cxb5 wins it, and neither ...Bb7 nor ...Bg7 gives enough in return, because g2 and d4 are both defended. White simply develops and takes the centre.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Gives away a pawn: after 3.dxe5 Bg7 4.Nf3 the e5-pawn is defended and the bishop's pressure achieves nothing, so White keeps the extra pawn.

1.c4 g6 2.d4 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn: 3.Bxg5 wins it, because the e7-pawn blocks the queen's diagonal and nothing else defends g5. The kingside is weakened for nothing.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop eyes the long diagonal towards c3 and b2 and Black can castle soon. Black commits to no pawn structure yet, which keeps every kind of game available, but White gets the first claim on space in the centre.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it covers e4 and d5. Black can still choose between a restrained set-up and an early challenge to the centre. The knight is committed before White has shown a plan, but nothing is conceded.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 c5.strategy: Takes d4 under control and mirrors White's play on the queenside, heading for a symmetrical game in which both sides fianchetto and fight for d4. Until ...Bg7 the diagonal to the h8-rook is open, so after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 the queen hits the rook, a tactic Black must keep in mind.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight, eyes d4 and e5 and supports a later ...e5. The knight blocks the c-pawn, though, and White can take space in the centre before Black has chosen a structure. Sound, but ...Bg7 first keeps more options open.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 behind a solid chain and closes the long diagonal at c6 before the bishop arrives. The centre is left to White for now, and the move commits the c-pawn before the set-up is known. Sound, but slow.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 d6.strategy: Frees the c8-bishop and prepares ...e5, which the g7-bishop will support, for a King's Indian-style set-up. It is sound but passive: the centre is left to White for now.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at c4 at once. After 3.cxd5 Nf6 Black regains the pawn with ...Nxd5, though Nc3 then hits the knight with gain of time. Taking back with 3...Qxd5 hits the rook on h1 instead, but 4.Nf3 blocks and Nc3 then drives the queen away.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 behind a solid chain and frees e7 for the knight. Once ...d5 is in, the e6-pawn shuts in the c8-bishop, while White takes space in the centre. Sound, but passive.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 e5.strategy: Takes space in the centre, with the bishop and a knight to support the pawn. The game becomes a closed one in which White controls d5 and plays on the queenside. Sound, but it commits Black to this structure early.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 f5.strategy: Controls e4 and heads for a set-up that develops the kingside quickly and castles early. It loosens e6 and commits the kingside pawns early. Sound, but double-edged.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but has little influence on the centre. White gains time to build in the centre.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 Bh6.strategy: Puts the bishop on h6 instead of g7, where White's c1-bishop meets it once d3 or d4 opens the diagonal. After Bxh6 Nxh6 Black has traded the dark-squared bishop that should guard f6 and h6, and the knight stands on the rim; avoiding the trade with ...Bg7 costs a tempo.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5, but the knight stands on the rim and e4 drives it away from there. It does nothing for the centre, and White simply builds there.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5, but that push would open the long diagonal to the a8-rook once White's bishop is on g2, so Black must first block it. Sound, but a tempo goes on a rim pawn that has no say in the centre.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and covers b4, but weakens b5 and develops nothing. It costs only a tempo, so it is sound, but White builds with a free hand.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 b6.strategy: Opens the long diagonal to the undefended rook on a8: after 3.Bg2 Black must block it at once, since the natural ...Bb7 loses the bishop to Bxb7. Each block leaves a later ...Bb7 behind Black's own piece or pawn, and the queenside is loosened.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight and blocks the diagonal of the future g7-bishop, while loosening e6 and the kingside. White can build in the centre at leisure.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 h6.strategy: Covers g5, a square White's c1-bishop cannot even reach until the d-pawn moves, and develops nothing. The g6-pawn loses the h-pawn's support.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 h5.strategy: Starts a kingside pawn push with ...h4 in mind, but loosens g5 and g6 and develops nothing. White answers with h4 or simply develops and takes the centre.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 g5.strategy: Pushes the g-pawn a second time, abandoning the fianchetto it prepared and leaving f5 and h5 without pawn cover. Once d3 or d4 opens the c1-bishop's diagonal, Bxg5 is threatened, and Black must spend another tempo defending the pawn.

1.c4 g6 2.g3 b5.strategy: Gives up a pawn to 3.cxb5. Black gets only the half-open b-file and the long diagonal for ...Bb7 in return, and White keeps the extra pawn by developing calmly.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, where it presses on the c3-knight and the b2-square, and clears f8 so that castling needs only the knight out. Black keeps every set-up open, but gives White time to take central space first.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight and watches d5 and e4. Black stays flexible between a fight against a White centre and a quieter manoeuvring game. The cost is that White decides how much space to take.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Controls d4 and heads for a symmetrical game, with the bishop on g7 next. Black fights for the centre from the flank and keeps the position balanced and manoeuvring. The cost is d5, which the c-pawn and the knight already cover and which Black can hardly contest.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Opens the c8-bishop's diagonal and covers c5 and e5, heading for a compact set-up with the bishop on g7 and a knight on f6. It is sound but not recommended: the d-pawn commits before the knights, the central strike with ...d5 is given up, and White takes central space before Black has chosen a plan.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight towards the centre, eyes d4 and e5 and supports a later ...e5. It blocks the c-pawn, though, so ...c5 is off while the knight stands there, and after 3.d4 the advance d5 can drive it away. Sound, but less flexible than developing the kingside first.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and reaches the position of 1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 g6, where ...Bg7 will guard e5. It is sound but not recommended: until the bishop arrives, the long diagonal to the h8-rook is open, so 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 hits the rook and White gains time.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with pawn support and reaches the position of 1.c4 c6 2.Nc3 g6. It is sound but not recommended: the pawn takes c6 from the b8-knight, and White can build a broad centre before ...d5 strikes at it.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 and frees e7 for the knight, reaching the position of 1.c4 e6 2.Nc3 g6. It is sound but not recommended: once ...d5 is in, the e6-pawn shuts in the c8-bishop, and the set-up is slow, so White can build the centre before Black has made a claim in it.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 and, with ...Bg7, a double fianchetto that aims both bishops at White's centre and queenside. It is sound but not recommended: neither knight is out yet, and White can take space before Black has settled on a set-up.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Controls e4 and heads for a set-up with a knight on f6, the bishop on g7 and early castling. It is sound but not recommended: the move weakens e6 and loosens the kingside before a piece is developed, and after 3.e4 fxe4 4.Nxe4 White's knight stands actively in the centre.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Offers a pawn that White can keep: after 3.cxd5 Nf6 4.e4 the d5-pawn is guarded by Nc3 and the e-pawn, so ...Nxd5 fails to exd5, and Black has no quick way to regain it.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim to reach b4 or c5, but it leaves the centre alone, and a3 chases ...Nb4 with a gain of time. White takes central space, and d4 also takes c5 from the knight.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 from the rim, but 3.e4 covers that square, and after 3.d4 the c1-bishop already eyes the knight. On h6 it does nothing for the centre while White takes it.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bh6.strategy: Puts the bishop on h6 instead of g7, where 3.d4 opens the c1-bishop's diagonal against it. A trade on h6 or c1 removes the dark-squared bishop the fianchetto was meant to serve, and retreating to g7 costs a tempo.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5, but takes f6 from the g8-knight, blocks the long diagonal of the coming ...Bg7 and weakens e6. Nothing is developed, and White builds a centre.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5, but the break does not work yet: ...b5 at once drops a pawn to cxb5 axb5 Nxb5. The tempo does nothing for the centre or development, and White builds the centre.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Controls b4 and gains a little queenside space, but develops nothing and weakens b5, which the a-pawn can no longer cover. White builds the centre undisturbed.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's c1-bishop, which cannot reach it while the d-pawn stands on d2, and leaves the g6-pawn without the h-pawn's support. Nothing is developed, and White builds a centre.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Prepares ...h4, but leaves the g6-pawn without the h-pawn's support, and the h-pawn can never again cover g5. Nothing is developed, and White builds a centre.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Pushes the g-pawn a second time, abandons the fianchetto it prepared and leaves f5 and h5 without pawn cover. Nothing guards g5, so 3.d4 threatens Bxg5, and Black must spend yet another tempo to save it.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Hangs a pawn: the c4-pawn and the c3-knight both attack b5 and nothing defends it, so 3.cxb5 or 3.Nxb5 simply wins it. Black has no lead in development to show for it.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, mirroring Black's set-up, and holds back the central pawns. White aims for a flexible, slower game in which the bishop on the long diagonal presses on d5 and the queenside, and the choice of central set-up stays open.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once: the pawns on c4 and e4, with the knight on c3 behind them, clamp the d5 square and give White a space advantage. Black has to challenge the centre with pieces and flank pawns, while White decides whether to build it up further or keep it closed.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with a second pawn at once. The pawn is guarded by the queen, so ...Bxd4 would give a bishop for a pawn. White gets space and a more open game, but the pawn becomes a target for the bishop on g7 and for a ...c5 break.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to a square that watches e4 and d5, the squares White's centre needs, and clears the way for castling. Black commits to nothing in the centre and stays flexible against White's slower build-up.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 c5.strategy: Takes control of d4 with a flank pawn before White has a centre, so a white d4 meets an immediate challenge. Black aims for a symmetrical, manoeuvring game in which the fight is over the d4 square and the queenside.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn and takes d4 and f4 away from White, so the game is likely to stay closed and slow. The pawn is guarded by the bishop on g7, which is blocked behind it for the time being, in return for space.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal at d5 and b7 and will shelter the castled king. The set-up is solid and flexible, and White fights for the centre with pieces first instead of occupying it at once.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight where it guards d4 and e5, and prepares castling once the bishop has gone to g2. White keeps every central plan open and gives nothing away, but takes no space yet and leaves Black free to choose the set-up.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Builds a pawn centre before the king's bishop is developed. It claims space, but Black can strike back in the centre at once, and White has to defend the central pawns with pieces that are not yet in play.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.Bg2 O-O.strategy: Brings the king to safety behind the bishop on g7 and the pawns on f7, g6 and h7 before the centre is decided. Black lets White commit first and keeps every plan in the centre available.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.Bg2 d6.strategy: Supports ...e5 and ...c5 and opens the diagonal of the c8 bishop. Black delays castling by a move at no cost and keeps a sturdy, flexible structure from which either central break can be chosen later.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.Bg2 c5.strategy: Takes control of d4 with a flank pawn before White has built a centre, so a white d4 meets an immediate challenge. Black aims for a symmetrical, manoeuvring game, and the fight is over the d4 square.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.Bg2 O-O 5.e.strategy: Takes space in the centre: pawns on c4 and e4 together clamp d5, and the knight on c3 backs up e4. White commits to a broad but slower centre, with d4 left for later, and Black's counterplay will aim at the d4 square.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.Bg2 O-O 5.N.strategy: Develops the knight where it guards d4 and e5, and clears the way for castling. White keeps every central plan available and waits to see how Black sets up, at the price of leaving the centre to be settled later.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.Bg2 O-O 5.d.strategy: Occupies the centre with a second pawn, defended only by the queen for now. The pawn is safe at the moment, since Black's bishop is shut in by its own knight. White gets space and an open game, and Black must strike at the pawn with a flank pawn or pieces.

1.c4 g6 2.Nc3 Bg7 3.g3 Nf6 4.Bg2 O-O 5.e.strategy: Fights for the centre in turn: the pawn supports a challenge with ...e5 or ...c5 and opens the diagonal of the c8 bishop. Black accepts a slightly cramped position in return for a sturdy, flexible structure.

Strikes at d4 with a flank pawn, so White cannot take the centre with d4 freely. Black accepts a weaker d5 square, which the pawns on c4 and e4 now control, in return for pressure on the queenside and a counter to the pawn centre.

Develops the knight to a square from which it watches d4 and e5. It blocks the c-pawn, so Black commits to meeting the centre with pieces and the e-pawn instead of a ...c5 break, and keeps a compact position.

Develops the knight to e2 rather than f3, which keeps the f-pawn free to advance and covers d4 and c3 from behind. White prepares castling and a space-gaining plan with the pawn centre, at the price of a knight that stands less actively than on f3.

The natural developing move: the knight guards d4 and e5 and clears the way for castling. It can be pinned against the queen by ...Bg4, and it blocks the f-pawn, so White plays for quick development more than for a flexible pawn push.

A modest, solid move: the pawn adds a guard to e4 and opens the diagonal of the c1 bishop. It spends a tempo without developing a piece and keeps the centre closed, so White plays for a slow manoeuvring game rather than for an advantage.
Takes control of d4 and f4 and claims space, so White cannot simply set up with d4. The centre is likely to stay closed, and both sides will manoeuvre for the d4 square and for a break on the flanks.

Develops the knight to a square from which it watches d4 and e5, and prepares ...e5. It blocks the c-pawn, so Black commits to a central pawn break with the e-pawn instead of a ...c5 break, and keeps a compact position.

Takes d4 under control with a flank pawn, so the knight on e2 cannot go there safely and White cannot advance in the centre freely. Black accepts a weaker d5 square, which the white knight on c3 can reach, in return for pressure on the queenside.
